title: AI Governance and Regulation Engineering Check

questions.question: What is the core invariant of an operational AI governance system?
options: Every material decision connects a system version and risk to an owner, evidence, control, decision, and follow-up action.
Every AI system uses the same control checklist.
A legal policy page exists before launch.
The model provider owns every downstream application risk.
questions.explanation: Traceable accountability lets a reviewer reconstruct what was assessed, who decided, which conditions applied, and what happened next.

questions.question: A safety evaluation passed for model v17, but production now uses model v18. What should the release gate conclude?
options: Approve because the model family name is unchanged.
Treat the evidence as version-mismatched and refresh or explicitly justify the affected claims before exposure.
Approve if the dashboard has no incidents yet.
Delete the old evaluation so reviewers are not confused.
questions.explanation: Evidence must identify the subject it supports. A report for a different version cannot silently authorize the candidate.

questions.question: How should an engineering team use the NIST AI RMF functions?
options: As connected, continuous outcomes adapted to context, with Govern cross-cutting Map, Measure, and Manage.
As four sequential tickets completed once.
As a legal classification produced entirely by a risk score.
As a replacement for product monitoring.
questions.explanation: NIST describes the functions as connected risk-management outcomes, not a one-size-fits-all ordered checklist.

questions.question: Why should EU AI Act dates and role mappings live in a maintained obligations catalog instead of application conditionals?
options: Because scope, guidance, and implementation schedules can change, while each decision must preserve the interpretation and source used at that time.
Because engineers never need to enforce controls.
Because every AI use case has identical duties.
Because legal interpretation eliminates the need for technical evidence.
questions.explanation: A maintained catalog can be reviewed and versioned without burying changing legal assumptions inside product code.

questions.question: A prompt change affects refusal behavior but not the model binary. Which review is most defensible?
options: No review because only model-weight changes are material.
Trace the prompt delta to documentation, quality, and safety claims, then rerun the smallest sufficient affected evidence set.
Rerun every organizational control regardless of impact.
Wait for a user complaint before recording the change.
questions.explanation: Materiality follows changed behavior and invalidated claims, not only model-weight changes.

questions.question: When is production monitoring valid governance evidence?
options: When each meaningful signal has version and cohort context, an owner, a threshold, and a response path.
When a dashboard contains many charts.
When raw prompts are retained forever.
When only aggregate satisfaction is measured.
questions.explanation: A signal becomes actionable evidence when it is attributable and tied to a decision boundary and accountable response.
